title: WFR-MFM: One-Step Inference for Dynamic Unbalanced Optimal Transport
claim: Learned dynamics recover both individual cell trajectories and population-level distributions, closely matching ground-truth data across time points.
layout: 2x2 grid; columns trajectories vs population, rows two datasets; shared legends
description: A 2x2 grid of scatter plots, labeled 'a' (left column) and 'b' (right column). The top row shows the Gene dataset and the bottom row shows the EMT dataset. Axes are Gene X1 and Gene X2. Points are colored from purple to yellow by time point: T0.0 to T4.0 on top, T0.0 to T3.0 on the bottom. Predicted cells are circles with black outlines. Ground-truth cells are faint X markers. In column a, thin gray lines trace individual cell trajectories from early to late clusters. In column b, resampled population distributions appear without lines. The top row shows a diagonal path of clusters from a dark purple blob at bottom right to a yellow cluster at top left. The bottom row shows a dense horizontal cloud that shifts from purple on the left to yellow on the right. Each panel has legends for time points and for marker meanings.
caption: Learned dynamics on the Gene and EMT datasets. Top: Gene dataset; bottom: EMT dataset. (a) Individual cell trajectories with evolving weights. (b) Population-level dynamics obtained by resampling cells according to normalized weights.
abstract: Reconstructing dynamical evolution from limited observations is a fundamental challenge in single-cell biology, where dynamic unbalanced optimal transport provides a principled framework for modeling coupled transport and mass variation. However, existing approaches rely on trajectory simulation at inference time, making inference a key bottleneck for scalable applications. In this work, we propose a mean-flow framework for unbalanced flow matching that summarizes both transport and mass-growth dynamics over arbitrary time intervals using mean velocity and mass-growth fields, enabling fast one-step generation without trajectory simulation. To solve dynamic unbalanced optimal transport under the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao geometry, we further build on this framework to develop Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao Mean Flow Matching (WFR-MFM). Across synthetic and real single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, WFR-MFM achieves orders-of-magnitude faster inference than a range of existing baselines while maintaining high predictive accuracy, and enables efficient perturbation response prediction on large synthetic datasets with thousands of conditions.
